Hazelcast diagnostics

Reading the report data…

    How this works

    • Files and members. Every file under the input folder that holds diagnostics sections is read (.log, .gz, …). A member is its address (host:port, from the file name or thisAddress); the start time in the file names separates its lifetimes (JVM runs), so counters never mix across a restart. The same file found twice is read once.
    • Times . Drag across any chart to zoom; every chart, table and number follows the range. Double-click a chart or press Zoom out to go back. Shaded areas have no data.
    • Metrics come from the MetricsPlugin dumps (every minute by default). Counters, which only grow (map.getCount, tcp.bytesReceived, gc.minorTime, …), are shown as a rate per second between two dumps of the same lifetime; a drop (restart) is skipped, not drawn as a negative rate. Everything else (sizes, used heap, pending counts) is a gauge, shown as the highest value in each time bin. The logs don't say which is which: names with words like size, pending, used, max are gauges; any other metric that never went down is a counter.
    • Data structures: maps, multimaps, replicated maps, caches, queues, topics, reliable topics, executors (executor.* with a name; the internal pools, executor.internal.*, are on the Operations tab), flake ID generators, PN counters… one kind at a time: a metric chart, a table of every structure of that kind (rates are averages per second and sizes the highest, in the time range in view) and, for the one you click, every metric it has. Lists and sets only report times (creation, last access), which are not charted. The CP Subsystem tab does the same for the CP objects (AtomicLong, FencedLock, semaphore, CountDownLatch, CPMap, CP sessions), named name@group.
    • Cleaning: for each metric of a data structure, a structure is left out when every value it had, on every member, is the same as its first one. Per-thread, per-pipeline and other per-item series that never changed are left out the same way (all-zero pipelines, for instance). Metrics that never changed are listed in the Unchanged table of their tab instead of drawn as flat lines.
    • Lines: By member draws one line per member (for per-map or per-thread metrics, the sum over all of them, or the max for percentages and maxima); By name / By operation draws one line per item, summed over the selected members. Colours follow the member, or the item's rank over the whole capture, so they don't change when you zoom or filter; items past the eighth are grey.
    • Latency comes from OperationsProfiler (time an operation ran on that member) and InvocationProfiler (end-to-end time of the invocations that member sent). Their counters are cumulative since the member started, so the first dump of each lifetime is a baseline and only the growth after it is counted. The profilers count calls in buckets that double in size (powers of 2 µs), so every boundary is one of 1.02 ms, 2.05 ms, 4.1 ms, 8.19 ms … 524 ms, 1.05 s, 2.1 s, 4.19 s, 8.39 s: 1.05 s and 2.1 s are the nearest to 1 s and 2 s. Each bucket from 1.02 ms up is kept for every interval, so the groups can be changed in the report: the fastest group (default < 4.1 ms), the slowest (default ≥ 524 ms) and the Slow from threshold (default 131 ms), which is always a group boundary; the boundaries in between are taken from 1.02, 4.1, 32.8, 131 and 524 ms, 1.05 and 2.1 s (at most six groups; five by default). Groups faster than the threshold are blue, the slow ones red. The Operation list picks one operation (it lists those that Find and the filters leave); a row of the table picks one row. A max is exact when the member's all-time max went up in that interval, otherwise an upper bound (≤). In the charts, an interval that spans two time slots is shared between them by overlap (so a slot can show 0.4 calls); the tables count each interval once, by its end.
    • WAN collects the wan.* metrics and the WAN traffic (tcp.*.WAN), and the latency of the WAN operations (classes in a wan package or named Wan…). The WAN publisher list keeps, in every chart and number of the tab, only the items of one publisher (publisherId and replication tags: its queue, its targets, its maps); the WAN bytes and the WAN operations are not per publisher. CP Subsystem collects the raft.* and cp.* metrics and the CP operations (cp or raft packages). Those operations stay on the Latency tab as well.
    • Slow operations come from the SlowOperations sections of the slow operation detector (every minute): each operation that ran on an operation thread for longer than its threshold (10 s by default), with the stack trace it was caught in, how many such invocations it counted, and the invocations it still keeps: start, duration so far, operation details. It lists them again at every dump for an hour after they last ran, so the report keeps each invocation once (by operation, start and identity hash), with the longest duration seen; one that ended less than 3 s before its member's last dump is marked still running. The end of an invocation is its start plus its duration.
    • Invocations come from the Invocations sections of the invocation sampler, written every hazelcast.diagnostics.invocation.sample.period.seconds when it is above 0. At each sample it goes through every invocation the member is waiting on (from the call until the response and the backup acknowledgements arrive) and adds one per operation to History, and to SlowHistory when it has been pending for longer than hazelcast.diagnostics.invocation.slow.threshold.seconds (5 s by default). Both count since the member started, so the growth from one dump to the next is the number pending at that sample; the first dump of each lifetime is the baseline, and a gap of several periods (a file missing) is shared out evenly. The slow ones are also listed with their details (Pending), the first hazelcast.diagnostics.invocation.slow.max.count - 1 (99) of them: an invocation listed at several dumps (its call id changes when it is retried) is shown once, from its first invocation to the last dump that listed it, with the longest duration seen. It is still pending at the member's last dump, or gone by the next dump, or not known when that dump's list was cut at 99. Past its call timeout, an invocation waits on because the target keeps answering its heartbeats: the operation is still queued or running there. The partition thread of a partition is partition-operation.thread- (partition id modulo operation.partitionThreadCount of the target).
    • MapStore comes from the MapStoreLatency sections (and QueueStoreLatency and the like), written when hazelcast.diagnostics.storeLatency.period.seconds is above 0: for each map and each method of its MapStore or MapLoader (load, loadAll, loadAllKeys, store, storeAll, delete, deleteAll), the same counters as the profilers: calls, total and max time, calls per power-of-2 µs bucket. They are cumulative since the member started, so the charts use the growth between two dumps, and the table Since the members started has the counters themselves. With hazelcast.diagnostics.storeLatency.reset.period.seconds the counters are reset after some dumps: a dump with a count, a total, a max or a bucket lower than at the dump before counts as reset, everything in it is new, and the totals keep what was counted before. The latency groups and the slow threshold are the Latency tab's.
    • GC logs found under the input folder are read too: JDK 9+ unified logging (-Xlog:gc*) and JDK 8 -XX:+PrintGCDetails. A line with a date-time (the time decoration, e.g. -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime, or -XX:+PrintGCDateStamps) is placed by it. A line with the JVM uptime only (the default decorations of -Xlog: uptime, level, tags) is placed with the JVM start of its member: in the diagnostics, the dump time minus runtime.uptime (without that metric, the lifetime's start in the file names, refined with the GC counts). Each JVM run of the log (at a restart the uptime starts again from 0) goes to the member's lifetime whose gc.minorCount lines up with its young pauses or, with no counts over it, whose diagnostics it overlaps; two runs that both start from 0 can't be one lifetime. A run that matches no lifetime isn't placed: the GC log files table counts its pauses. With GC logs alone and the uptime only, the time axis is the JVM uptime (0 is each JVM's start) and each JVM has a line of its own. A GC log goes with the member whose diagnostics or member logs are in the same folder; else with the member whose host name (and port) is in the GC log's file name, then in its folder names (gc_logs_uklpapscl101a/gc.log); else with the one in the nearest folder, and when several are as near, the one whose lifetime started with that JVM (wall time minus uptime). A GC log that matches no member gets a line of its own on the GC tab, but it isn't counted as a member. Rotated files and copies are read once (by JVM run and GC id). Each pause is a dot on the GC tab, coloured by its kind: young and mixed, remark / cleanup / other, and the ones caused by a humongous allocation; full GCs and evacuation failures (to-space exhausted) are marked with a red line and cross. The heap is the one printed on the pause line (before → after (committed)); the time in pauses is the pauses' sum over the time the member has a GC log.
    • Stuck threads are checked at every metrics dump, for every thread of every member: a thread is stuck when it stays idle while its queue stays above 0, at two dumps in a row at least. For an IO thread (tcp.inputThread, tcp.outputThread): tasks wait in its queue (taskQueueSize > 0) and it did no I/O since the dump before (idleTimeMillis at least 90% of the time since that dump). For a partition or generic operation thread: operations wait for it (normalPendingCount + priorityPendingCount > 0) and it completed none since the dump before (completedTotalCount unchanged). An episode starts at the thread's last I/O (from idleTimeMillis), or at the dump before when nothing was waiting there yet, and ends at the last dump with work waiting, so its end is only as precise as the dump period. Threads that are idle with an empty queue, or busy with a queue, are not stuck.
    • Transfer: each connection has its own byte counters in the metrics (tcp.connection.in.bytesRead, tcp.connection.out.bytesWritten, named local address->remote address). A member's connection is matched to another member when that member has the same connection going out (same ports); a connection a member opened to an address outside the cluster goes to another cluster (WAN replication). The others are clients, by host; their type (Java, C++, .NET, Python, Management Center…) and WAN replication coming in from another cluster are known when the metrics include tcp.connection.connectionType (DEBUG level). The member totals come from the IO threads (tcp.inputThread / outputThread.bytesTransceived), which also count the connections that opened and closed between two dumps (not seen as a connection). A counter's first dump in a lifetime is its baseline, and growth across a gap in the dumps is left out.
    • Measure: pick Drag to: Measure in the toolbar (or hold Shift while dragging), then drag across any chart, or type the times; every chart then shows what went through that span: the bytes for byte counters (rates added up over time), the count for other counters and the profilers, the average and max for sizes. The Transfer tab's amounts follow the span. Escape or Clear removes it. Amounts are as precise as the dumps: at the edges of the span, a dump interval counts for the part inside.
    • Saturated executors (Operations tab) are checked at every metrics dump, for every executor with a queueSize, a poolSize and a maximumPoolSize (executor.internal.* and the like): saturated when its pool is full (poolSize ≥ maximumPoolSize) and tasks wait in its queue (queueSize > 0), at two dumps in a row at least.
    • Member logs. The members' own logs found in the input folder (hazelcast.log, console output, rotated and .gz files; java.util.logging, log4j, log4j2 and logback layouts) are read too. A log belongs to the member whose address its lines print ([host]:port); a member with logs but no diagnostics gets its own entry. Their tabs (Source: Member logs, in purple) chart the HealthMonitor lines, every exception grouped by class and root cause, OutOfMemoryError (also marked on every chart of both sources), the lines that matter (thread starvation and clock leaps, system clock jumps, suspected members, quorum and split-brain protection failures, split brain and merges, slow and delayed operations, closed connections, lifecycle and membership) and the CP Subsystem: groups, roles, terms, elections, sessions, persistence. Times are the ones printed in the logs (converted when a line has a zone offset), so they line up with the diagnostics when both were written in the same time zone.
